One child: call one person. Two to four children: each interviews a different person, then compare tables. Many families know something. In Kerala some people keep stingless bees in a small log or a coconut shell. Termite mounds, mud tubes on walls and wasp nests under roofs are common across India. If nobody you know has seen any, ask a neighbour, a gardener or a shopkeeper.
flow.context: In this step you interview someone and collect what they know about social insects.

flow.do: Read your table. Mark each place on a small sketch map. Ask your child what the older person knew that surprised them.
flow.say: Read your table back. What surprised you? Which insect did the person know the most about? Mark the places on a map.
flow.kid: Read your table. Mark the places on a map. What surprised you?
flow.think: What does one person's knowledge miss that a whole village's knowledge might have?
flow.context: This is the last step of Ask the Elders. You collect your findings and mark them on a map.

activities.title: Huddle or Spread: how a crowd keeps warm

materials.item: 6 small identical bottles with lids, about 200 to 300 millilitres each (small plastic water or juice bottles are best)
bath-warm water, about 40 degrees Celsius: mix hot and cold tap water until it feels pleasantly warm on your wrist
rubber bands or string, to tie three bottles together
a digital fever thermometer, the kind used for children (most homes have one; a medical shop sells one for about Rs 100 to 150)
a table in the coolest room of the house, away from the fan, the window and the sun

activities.safety: A grown-up fills the bottles with bath-warm water. Do not use boiling or very hot water. It can scald, and it can crack glass or bend a plastic bottle. Wash the thermometer with soap and water afterwards, and do not use it for a fever until it is clean.

schedule.what: Fill six bottles with the same warm water. Tie three in a bundle and space three apart. After 20 minutes, check which are warmer.

activities.record: A table with the temperature (or the result of the blind hand test) of the middle bottle in the bundle and of a lone bottle, at the start and after 20 minutes, and how many degrees each one fell.
activities.context: In this activity you test why a crowd of bees keeps warmer in a tight bundle than spread out. In a cold place, honeybees cluster together to stay warm.

setup.art: Six identical bottles of warm water on a table, with three tied together in a bundle and three standing apart.
setup.caption: 1. Fill six identical bottles with the same warm water. Tie three in a bundle.

setup.art: A thermometer or a hand held against a bottle in the middle of the bundle, and against a bottle standing alone.
setup.caption: 2. Check the middle bottle and a lone bottle at the start.

setup.art: The same table twenty minutes later, with a child checking the middle bottle in the bundle and the lone bottle.
setup.caption: 3. After 20 minutes check them again.

flow.do: Show your child the six bottles. Say that three will be tied in a bundle and three will stand apart. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Bees in a cold place cluster tightly together. We will see if a bundle keeps warm better than bottles standing alone. Which will be warmer in twenty minutes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three bottles in a bundle. Three bottles alone. Which stays warmer? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will stay warmer?
good: Bottles in a bundle keep each other warm.
The ones in the middle have less open air around them.
Bottles alone lose heat to the air.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Huddle or Spread. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up fills all six bottles with the same warm tap water, up to the same line. Put the lids on. Tie three bottles into a bundle. Space the other three apart on the table.
flow.say: A grown-up fills all six bottles from the same tap. Put on the lids. Tie three bottles in a tight bundle. Put the other three well apart.
flow.kid: A grown-up fills six bottles. Tie three in a bundle. Put three apart.
flow.parent: The water should be the same in every bottle, so fill them one after another from the same tap. The bundle should be as tight as you can tie it.

check.q: Why do all six bottles get the same warm water?
options: So only the arrangement can make a difference
So the bundle gets heavier
So the water looks the same
check.why: If one bottle began warmer, it could stay warmer for that reason alone. When everything else is the same, a difference after 20 minutes comes from the bundle or the space.

flow.context: In this step a grown-up fills the bottles, and you set up the bundle and the single bottles.

flow.do: Open the lid and put the thermometer tip into the middle bottle of the bundle, then into one lone bottle. Wait for the beep, write the value, and close the lid. Do both within one minute, always the bundle first. If you have no thermometer, do the hand test described in the note.
flow.say: Check the middle bottle of the bundle, and one lone bottle. Write what you find. Use a thermometer, or the back of your hand.
flow.kid: Check the middle bottle and a lone bottle. Write what you find.
flow.parent: Use the same thermometer for both and do them in the same order at the end. The middle bottle is the one with a bottle on each side of it. Without a thermometer, use a blind hand test: one person closes their eyes, another puts the same palm on the bundle bottle and a lone bottle for five seconds each, in a random order, and the first person says which is warmer. One child: the parent mixes up the bottles. Two to four children: one child reads the thermometer, one writes, and others do the blind test, then swap.
flow.context: In this step you write the starting temperatures.

flow.do: Leave the bottles for 20 minutes in total. While you wait, draw the two arrangements, and mark where you think the heat is going.
flow.say: Wait twenty minutes. While you wait, draw both arrangements. Mark with arrows where you think the heat is going.
flow.kid: Wait. Draw both. Add arrows for where the heat goes.
flow.parent: Keep the bottles away from the fan, the window and the sun. Twenty minutes in total is the aim, so a few minutes from step 3 count towards this.
flow.context: In this step you wait and draw what you think is happening to the heat.

flow.do: Check the middle bottle of the bundle and a lone bottle again. Write the values. Ask your child what they found and why.
flow.say: Check the middle bottle and a lone bottle again. Which is warmer? How much? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Check the two bottles again. Which is warmer? Why?
flow.parent: A bundle usually stays warmer, because the middle bottle has fewer open sides to lose heat from. A typical difference is about one degree after 20 minutes, and it can be even smaller in a hot room, where the water is already close to the air temperature. If the two read within 0.3 degree, you can say there was no clear difference, and try again in a cooler room or early morning. In hot weather you can also turn the test round: start with fridge-cold water and see which bottle warms up more slowly. Write exactly what you found.
flow.think: Honeybees in a cold place shiver their muscles to make heat. Why does it help them to be in a tight ball?
flow.context: This is the last step of Huddle or Spread. You check the bottles and say what you found.

projects.title: Our Home as a Colony: three days of jobs

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
coloured pencils
everyone who lives in your home, for a short talk each day

projects.safety: Choose a job for the swap that is safe for you, such as watering plants, laying the table, sorting washing or sweeping. Leave out jobs with a stove, a knife or electricity unless a grown-up is beside you.

schedule.what: List every job done in your home in one day, and who does each. Draw the table.
Pick a person who is usually at home and could be away for a day (not someone whose absence makes the family sad). Plan who takes over their jobs, and what each swap will need.
Do one job swap for an hour. Talk about what was easy, what took time, and what you learned.

projects.record: A job table with who does each job, a swap plan, and a note about one hour of swapping.
projects.context: In this project you study your own home as if it were a colony. You find out who does which jobs, how the jobs would change if someone were away, and what it takes to learn a new job.

setup.art: A page with a table: Job, Who does it, How long it takes, How often.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table of the jobs in your home.

setup.art: A child talking to a family member at the kitchen table and writing in the notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Ask each person what jobs they do in a day.

setup.art: A child and an adult swapping a small job, such as watering plants, with a timer on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Swap one safe job for an hour.

flow.do: Draw a table with four columns: the job, who does it, how long it takes, and how often. Walk around the home and write down at least ten jobs.
flow.say: Every home has jobs. Cooking, sweeping, washing, shopping, watering, helping with homework. Let's write them all down. Who does each one?
flow.kid: Draw your table. Walk round your home. List ten jobs.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Home as a Colony. You list the jobs in your home.

flow.do: Ask each person at home which jobs they do and how long each takes. Fill in the table. Colour the jobs of each person in a different colour.
flow.say: Ask each person which jobs they do, and how long each one takes. Write it in. Colour each person's jobs in their own colour.
flow.kid: Ask each person their jobs. Fill in the table. Use one colour for each person.

ask.q: Do jobs go with age, with skill, or with who is at home?
good: Some jobs are for older people.
Some jobs go to whoever is at home.
People change jobs when something changes.

flow.parent: Let everyone speak. Do not turn this into a discussion about who works harder. It is a study, not a score.
flow.context: In this step you collect everyone's jobs and show them in colour.

flow.do: Pick one person who could be away tomorrow, for a pretend day. Plan who takes over each of their jobs. Write what each swap needs, such as learning a skill or finding time.
flow.say: Suppose one person is away tomorrow. Who does their jobs? What does each swap need? Does anyone need to learn something first?
flow.kid: Suppose one person is away. Plan who takes over their jobs.

ask.q: Which job would be hardest to swap, and why?
good: One that needs a skill.
One that takes a long time to learn.
One that only one person knows how to do.

flow.parent: This is the same problem a hive has when foragers are lost. A home, like a hive, needs several people who can do each job.

check.q: A home has one person who knows how to pay the bills, and nobody else. What is the risk?
options: If that person is away, the job is not done
The job is done faster
Nobody else wants to do it
check.why: Sharing jobs between specialists saves time, but it has a risk. If only one member can do a job and is missing, the job stops. Hives and homes both manage the risk by letting members learn each other's jobs.

flow.context: In this step you plan how your home would manage if one person were away.

flow.do: Choose one safe job to swap for an hour. The child does an adult's job, and an adult does one of the child's jobs. Use a timer, and note how long the swapped job takes.
flow.say: Today we swap one job for an hour. You do one of my jobs, and I do one of yours. Note how long it takes. Is it as quick for you as for the usual person?
flow.kid: Swap one safe job for an hour. Use a timer. Is it quicker or slower?
flow.parent: Choose a small job. The adult should do the child's job in the child's way, and not correct it. One child: swap with one adult. Two to four children: each child swaps with a different family member, or takes turns, and the others time. Do not swap any job with a stove, a knife or electricity.
flow.context: In this step you swap one job and time it.

flow.do: Talk about the swap. What was easy? What took time? Did the swap change how you see the job?
flow.say: How did the swap go? What took time? What would help the next person learn this job faster?
flow.kid: How did the swap go? What took time? What would help?
flow.parent: Do not turn this into a judgement of who did well. The point is to see that jobs take learning, that swapping has a cost, and that a home works better when many people can do many jobs.
flow.think: In a hive, a bee changes jobs as she ages. Do people in your home change jobs as they get older?
flow.context: This is the last step of Our Home as a Colony. You talk about what the swap showed.

challenges.title: The Cool Nest: keep a shoebox nest cooler on a hot day
challenges.problem: Termites and bees must keep their nests from getting too hot. Termite mounds are built with tunnels and thick walls, and honeybees fan their wings at the door. Design a shoebox nest that keeps an ice cube from melting for as long as you can in a sunny window, using only things you find at home.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Use shoeboxes or similar cardboard boxes of the same size. One stays plain, as the comparison, and each design gets its own box.
Use an ice cube of the same size in a steel katori in each box. Take the cubes out of the freezer only when everything else is ready.
The lid must stay on, but you may cut up to four small holes, each as wide as a finger.
Never use a flame or a hot stove.
materials: 3 shoeboxes or similar cardboard boxes of the same size, with lids (one plain, up to two designs)
3 ice cubes of the same size from one ice tray (or ice from a nearby shop kept in a flask)
a teaspoon and a small glass, to measure the meltwater
kitchen foil, white paper, newspaper, tape, scissors
a sunny window sill, or a table under a bright lamp
general: Cover the whole box with foil, shiny side out, to reflect the sunlight.
Line the inside of the box with crumpled newspaper, so heat has a harder time getting in.
Paint or cover the outside with white paper, because white reflects more light.
creative: Cut two holes, one low and one high, and fit straw chimneys, so warm air can leave at the top and cooler air can come in below.
Make a double wall of cardboard with an air gap between, like a termite mound's thick wall.
Put the box on an upturned tray and a wet cloth, so water evaporating takes heat away.
challenges.your_turn: Test two of your own ideas, each in its own box against the plain box, in the same window for 20 minutes. Then pour the meltwater from each katori into a small glass, and count the teaspoons. The box with the least meltwater kept its ice best. Pick the best, and say why it works.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about how a nest stays cool. You build a shoebox nest with tricks like termites and bees, and test it by seeing how much ice is left.

setup.art: Two identical shoeboxes with lids on a sunny window sill, one plain and one wrapped in foil with two straw chimneys.
setup.caption: 1. Prepare a plain box and a box with your design.

setup.art: An ice cube in a steel katori inside each box, with a hand placing the lid.
setup.caption: 2. Put one ice cube of the same size in a katori inside each box.

setup.art: A child opening both boxes after twenty minutes and comparing the two katoris, one with more ice left.
setup.caption: 3. After 20 minutes, open both boxes and compare the ice.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask how termites and bees keep a nest cool. List the ideas on paper.
flow.say: A termite mound and a beehive both have to stay cool in the Indian summer. How could a nest lose heat or stop heat from getting in? List some ideas.
flow.kid: How could a nest stay cool? Think of ideas.

ask.q: What helps you stay cool on a hot day?
good: A fan.
White clothes.
Shade.
Water.

flow.parent: Termites build mounds with tunnels that let air move through, and bees fan their wings at the door. In a flat you can copy the idea with vents and covers.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Cool Nest. You think about the problem.

flow.do: Build your design in one box. Leave one box plain. If you have a third box, build a second, different idea in it. Cut up to four small holes in a designed box. A grown-up cuts the holes. Do not touch the plain box.
flow.say: Choose your ideas. Build them into one box. Leave the other plain. You may cut up to four small holes.
flow.kid: Build your design in one box. Leave one plain.
flow.parent: Help only with scissors. Let your child decide on the design. A design that does not work is still a result.
flow.context: In this step you build your nest design.

flow.do: Put both boxes side by side in the same sunny window, or under the same bright lamp. A grown-up puts an ice cube in each katori and the katoris in the boxes, with the lids on. Wait 20 minutes.
flow.say: Put the boxes side by side in the same sunny place. Put one ice cube in each katori and close the lids. Wait twenty minutes. Meanwhile, guess which will have more ice.
flow.kid: Put both boxes in the sun. Add an ice cube to each. Wait 20 minutes.
flow.parent: Both boxes must get the same sun, so keep them level and next to each other. A lamp can be hot, so keep it away from paper and foil. Two to four children: each child builds one design box, and all designs share the one plain box; take turns to put in the ice and to measure. In a hot month a plain cube can almost melt in 20 minutes; if both katoris are nearly empty, repeat with a larger ice block. Typically a foil-covered box keeps a little more ice, and an honest result of no difference is also worth writing down.

check.q: Why do both katoris get an ice cube of the same size?
options: So the amount of ice is a fair comparison
So the katoris look alike
So the ice melts at the same speed
check.why: If one cube started bigger, it would last longer for that reason alone. Keeping the cubes the same lets any difference come from the nest design.

flow.context: In this step you test your design in the heat.

flow.do: Open both boxes. Look at each katori. Which has more ice left? Pour each katori's meltwater into a glass and count the teaspoons. Ask what made the difference.
flow.say: Open both boxes. Which katori has more ice left? What did your design do? What would you change?
flow.kid: Open the boxes. Which has more ice? What would you change?

ask.q: What do you think kept your ice from melting, or let it melt?
good: The foil reflected the sun.
The holes let warm air out.
The paper kept the heat out.

flow.think: A termite mound has no fan. How could a building move air without one?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Cool Nest. You compare your design with the plain box and say why.

items.p: What is a colony?
opts: The whole family of an ant, bee, wasp or termite society, living in one nest
A single worker bee
A kind of flower that bees visit
A large group of different kinds of insects that happen to meet
items.why: A colony is the whole society living in one nest, with a queen, workers and young. A single bee is only one member of the colony. Strangers who meet at a flower are not a colony.

items.p: In a honeybee hive, the female who lays all the eggs is called the ____.
a: queen
items.why: The queen lays the eggs. The workers are her daughters, and they almost never lay eggs. She does not give orders.

items.p: Match each honeybee word to its meaning.
pairs: lays all the eggs of the hive
a male bee who mates with a queen from another hive
flies out to find nectar and pollen
looks for something new, such as a home, and reports back
stands at the door and sniffs each arrival
items.why: These five words come up all through the unit. Knowing them lets you explain what each bee in a hive does.

items.p: Sort these bee jobs. Is each one done inside the hive, or away from the hive?
items: cleaning empty cells
Inside the hive
feeding a grub
Inside the hive
packing pollen into a cell
Inside the hive
flying to a field of flowers
Away from the hive
searching for a new home for a swarm
Away from the hive
flying home with nectar from a mango orchard
Away from the hive
items.why: Cleaning, feeding and packing happen in the dark hive, usually by younger bees. Foraging and searching for a home happen outside, usually by older bees.

items.p: The queen honeybee tells each worker which job to do.
items.why: False. The queen lays eggs but does not give orders. A worker's job changes with her age and with what the hive needs, which she senses from smells, touch and the state of the hive.

items.p: Put the jobs of a worker honeybee in the usual order, from the youngest age to the oldest.
items: Cleaning empty cells
Feeding the grubs
Building wax and storing food
Guarding the door
Flying out to find food
a: Cleaning empty cells
Feeding the grubs
Building wax and storing food
Guarding the door
Flying out to find food
items.why: A worker usually starts inside the hive and ends outside. Foraging is the last job, and also the most dangerous.

items.p: A child timed two ways of doing a three-step job on 12 paper squares, two rounds each. The bars show the total time for each way. Which way was faster, and by how much?
opts: One step at a time, by 30 seconds
One square at a time, by 30 seconds
One step at a time, by 544 seconds
They took the same time
items.why: A shorter bar means less time, so one step at a time was faster. 287 minus 257 is 30 seconds. The other options add the bars or read the wrong bar.

items.p: A hive splits its jobs among many bees, but its bees can also change jobs. Write two sentences to say why a hive needs both.
items.a: Splitting jobs means each bee gets a lot of practice and does not waste time swapping jobs. But if the hive loses all its foragers and no bee can change jobs, nobody brings food. So it helps that bees can change jobs when the hive needs it.
items.why: A strong answer names the gain of splitting jobs, which is practice and less time lost swapping, and the risk, which is that a job is left undone if nobody can take it over.

items.p: A termite soldier can change into a worker if the colony needs more workers.
items.why: False. A termite soldier grows up with a big hard head and large jaws, built for defence. She or he keeps that job for life. Honeybee workers are different, because they can change jobs.

items.p: Here is a picture of a honeybee dancing on the comb. Label the three parts: the line pointing straight up, the waggle run, and the angle between them.
a: Line pointing straight up: the direction of the Sun
The waggle run: the straight line she walks while shaking, which shows the direction of the food
The angle between them: how far to the left or right of the Sun the food is
items.why: Straight up on the comb stands for the Sun's direction. The angle of the waggle run from straight up is the angle between the Sun and the food.
items.art: A honeybee on a vertical honeycomb running a straight line that leans to the right of a dotted line pointing straight up.

items.p: Three of these animals live in eusocial societies, with a queen and workers. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Honeybee
Termite
Naked mole-rat
Indian elephant
items.why: Honeybees, termites and naked mole-rats have one breeding female and many helpers. An Indian elephant herd is led by an older female, but most grown females can have calves.

items.p: Draw the door of a beehive and three bees at it. Show a guard, a bee that is fanning her wings, and a forager coming home with pollen. Write one label for each.
items.a: A hive door with three bees. The guard stands at the door facing a bee that has just arrived. The fanning bee has her wings blurred, and she stands at the entrance. The forager has yellow lumps on her back legs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows each bee doing something different at the same door. That is division of labour at a single spot.
items.art: A blank box with a sketch of a wooden beehive door at the bottom.

items.p: A hive has 30,000 bees. About 1 in 3 are foragers right now. How many foragers is that?
items.why: One third of 30,000 is 30,000 divided by 3, which is 10,000. The other 20,000 are doing jobs inside the hive.

items.p: A swarm of bees has settled on the grill of a balcony in a block of flats. The residents are deciding what to do.

views.says: Swarms are dangerous. We should drive them away with smoke and water, right now.
A swarm is usually gentle, because the bees carry no honey to defend. Leave them alone for a day or two, and then a beekeeper can collect them.
Let them stay and watch. The scouts are choosing a home, and we can watch how.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what you would want to find out first.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit, such as that a swarm has no store to defend, or that the bees will choose a home and leave on their own.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. Swarms can sting if attacked, and they are usually gentle if left alone. A good answer uses what we know about swarms, and says what else we would need to check.

items.p: Scientists say 'caste' for the groups in an insect society. How is this different from caste among people?
opts: In biology it means a group with one kind of job or body in an insect colony, and has nothing to do with the caste system among people
They mean exactly the same thing
Insect castes are decided by which family you are born in
Human castes are decided by the jobs you do as you grow up
items.why: In biology 'caste' names a type of worker, soldier or queen in an insect society. The caste system among people divides families by birth and has been used unfairly. A honeybee changes her job as she ages, and a person should not be held to a job by their birth.

worksheets.title: How Groups Share Work and Decide (stretch)

items.p: In a small pin factory, ten workers each did one or two steps of the work. Together they made about 48,000 pins in a day. About how many pins did each worker help to make?
opts: About 4,800
About 480
About 48
About 48,000
items.why: 48,000 divided by 10 is 4,800. One person doing every step alone might make only a few dozen in a day. Sharing the steps gave far more pins for each person.

items.p: Why can a termite soldier not be turned into a worker when a colony needs more workers?
opts: Her body was built for defence, with a hard head and large jaws
Soldiers refuse to do the work
The queen forbids it
Workers are always bigger than soldiers
items.why: A termite soldier grows up with a body built for one job. Her caste is part of her body, not only a job that she does. A honeybee's job is different. It changes as she ages.

items.p: A scientist takes all the older bees out of a hive and leaves only young bees. Say what you expect the young bees to do, and explain why.
items.a: Some of the young bees will start foraging earlier than usual. A hive with no foragers has no food coming in, and the missing foragers' job gets taken over by bees who are young for it.
items.why: A strong answer names the change in jobs and says that the hive's need, not a bee's age alone, set the change. Huang and Robinson found this in 1992.

items.p: A swarm's queen decides which hollow tree the swarm will move into.
items.why: False. The scouts decide through their dances, and the swarm moves when enough scouts are at one place. The queen stays in the middle of the swarm.

items.p: Put the steps of a swarm's choice in order, from the first to the last.
items: Scouts fly out and find possible homes
Scouts come back and dance for the homes they found
Dances for better homes grow, and dances for poorer homes fade
About fifteen scouts gather at one home
The swarm warms up and flies to that home
a: Scouts fly out and find possible homes
Scouts come back and dance for the homes they found
Dances for better homes grow, and dances for poorer homes fade
About fifteen scouts gather at one home
The swarm warms up and flies to that home
items.why: Each step needs the one before it. The choice grows out of many scouts doing small things, and the quorum is the signal to go.

items.p: The smallest number of members who must agree before a group acts is called the ____.
a: quorum
items.why: Honeybee swarms use a quorum of about fifteen scouts at one site before they take off. Many human groups, such as a school committee, use quorums too.

items.p: Five people guessed how many chana were in a glass. The guesses, in order, were 120, 250, 280, 310 and 650. The true number was 300. How many of the five guesses were closer to 300 than the middle guess?

chart.title: Five guesses for a glass of chana (made-up)

opts: None
One
Three
All of them
items.why: The middle guess is 280, which is 20 from 300. Only the guess of 310 is closer, at 10. The other three are further away, so the middle guess beat four of the five people but not all.

items.p: Sort each situation. Will a crowd's middle guess probably be close to the true number, or probably be wrong?
items: Everyone guesses alone, and some guess too high while others guess too low
Probably close
Everyone copies the first person's guess
Probably wrong
A trick makes every jar look half as full as it is
Probably wrong
Fifty people with different ideas each guess in secret
Probably close
items.why: A crowd cancels out mistakes that go in different directions. It cannot cancel out a mistake that everyone shares, such as copying or a trick that fools everyone the same way.

items.p: Three of these help to hold an ant or bee colony together. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A smell shared by the whole colony
Food passed from mouth to mouth
A queen who gives orders to every worker
Warmth made by many bees together
items.why: A shared smell, shared food and shared warmth really do hold colonies together. The queen does not give orders. She lays eggs, and the workers respond to what they sense in the hive.

items.p: At one moment, half the ants in a nest are standing still. Give two possible reasons for this, and say which one you find more believable and why.
items.a: One reason is that the standing ants are a reserve, ready to join in if the colony needs more workers. Another is that workers take turns resting, so the colony does not run out of workers all at once. I find the reserve idea easier to believe, because a colony with ants ready to go can react quickly. But scientists have not shown which is true.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons and says that scientists have not settled it. Either choice is fine if it comes with a reason.

items.p: Match each society to something that belongs to its way of life.
pairs: a chain of diggers passing soil backwards
a fungus garden that feeds the whole colony
a dance that tells others the direction of food
a pouch for sharing food mouth to mouth
a nest of paper made from chewed wood
items.why: Eusocial animals work together in different ways. They share the idea of a few breeders and many helpers, but their jobs and tools are different.

items.p: Here is a picture of a field map. The hive is at the bottom, the Sun's direction is a line going up, and a field of flowers is to the right. Label the three things.
a: Hive: where the dance happens
Direction of the Sun: the line that straight up on the comb stands for
Flower field: the place the dance describes, to the right of the Sun's direction
items.why: A dancer turns the position of a field into an angle on the comb. The hive is the starting point, and the Sun's direction is the line that the angle is measured from.
items.art: A top-down map with a hive at the bottom, a dotted line going up marked with a Sun, and a field of flowers up and to the right.

items.p: Draw two bee dances on the comb. One is for flowers close to the hive, and one is for flowers very far away. Show what is different.
items.a: Two combs. On the first, a short waggle run. On the second, a much longer waggle run. Both runs lean at some angle from straight up.
items.why: The length of the waggle run tells the distance. A short run means near. A long run means far.
items.art: Two blank squares for two honeycomb pictures, side by side.

items.p: Is a honeybee hive one animal or thousands of animals?

views.who: A scientist who studies whole colonies
views.says: A hive keeps its own warmth, feeds its young, and has offspring by swarming. It acts like one body.

views.who: A scientist who studies single bees
views.says: Each bee has her own body and her own senses. A hive is thousands of animals following their own rules.
Maybe it is both, depending on what you want to ask about.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing the other view gets right.
items.a: Any view with a reason, such as that a hive keeps its warmth together, or that each bee flies alone.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Both views describe something true. 'One animal' captures what the hive does together, and 'thousands of animals' captures what each bee is.

items.p: Some ants stand still while others work. Which result would best support the idea that the still ants are a reserve?
opts: When a large piece of food appears, many of the still ants join in at once
The still ants never move at all, for days
The still ants are always the youngest ants
The still ants die first when the colony is short of food
items.why: A reserve is a group that waits and then acts when needed. If still ants join in when there is more work, that fits. Ants that never move, or that are only the young or dying, would suggest other explanations.

worksheets.title: Queens, Quorums and What We Cannot Conclude (challenge)

items.p: Naked mole-rats are mammals, and they live with a queen and many helpers. What does this tell us about eusocial life?
opts: It has appeared in very different animals, not only in insects
It only works for animals with six legs
It only works for animals that fly
It is the usual way mammals live
items.why: Eusociality has appeared on Earth more than a dozen separate times, in insects, shrimp and mammals. It is rare, but it is not limited to one body type.

items.p: Naked mole-rats and humans are both mammals. Give one big difference between a human society and a mole-rat colony, and say what you cannot conclude from the mole-rats about how people should live.
items.a: In a human village, nearly every adult can have children, but in a mole-rat colony only the queen and a few males do. We cannot conclude that people should have a queen or a ruler, because what happens in nature does not tell us what is fair for people.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real difference and says that a fact about animals does not tell us what people should do. Naked mole-rats are one example of how life can be arranged, not a rule.

items.p: Because honeybee hives have a queen, it is natural and so right for people to have rulers.
items.why: False. Just because something happens in nature does not make it right or fair for people. Elephants are led by older females, wolf packs are families, and most animals live alone.

items.p: A child did four rounds of a paper-square job in this order: one square at a time, one step at a time, one step at a time, one square at a time. The chart shows the times. Why did the child use this order?

data.label: Round 1, one square at a time
Round 2, one step at a time
Round 3, one step at a time
Round 4, one square at a time

opts: So that getting faster with practice affects both ways equally
So that the first way always wins
So that the child can stop early
So that the last round is the shortest
items.why: People usually get quicker with practice. If one way always came first and the other second, practice could help the second way. Putting each way early once and late once spreads the effect of practice across both ways.

items.p: Sort each job. Is it done by a body built for it, or by a bee whose job changes with age and need?
cats: Job changes with age and need
items: A termite soldier blocking a tunnel
Body built for the job
A honeybee foraging at 25 days old
Job changes with age and need
A young bee that forages early after a storm
Job changes with age and need
A big-headed ant cutting hard seeds
Body built for the job
items.why: Some insects have different bodies for different castes, and a soldier stays a soldier. In honeybees all workers have the same kind of body, and the job depends on age and on what the hive needs.

items.p: Put these colonies in order, from the fewest animals to the most.
items: A small paper wasp nest, about 30 wasps
A naked mole-rat colony, about 75 animals
A honeybee hive, about 30,000 bees
A big termite mound, millions of termites
a: A small paper wasp nest, about 30 wasps
A naked mole-rat colony, about 75 animals
A honeybee hive, about 30,000 bees
A big termite mound, millions of termites
items.why: The sizes of colonies vary enormously. Termite mounds can hold millions, honeybee hives tens of thousands, and mole-rat colonies and wasp nests only dozens.

items.p: Why does a swarm wait for a quorum of scouts before it flies, instead of going as soon as one scout says she has found a home?
items.a: One scout may have found a poor home or made a mistake. If about fifteen scouts have all checked the same place themselves, the choice is much more likely to be good. A quorum protects the swarm from one scout's mistake.
items.why: A strong answer says that one scout can be wrong and that many independent checks make the choice safer.

items.p: A scout dances very long for a poor hollow. In real swarms, why does this usually not drag the swarm into a poor home?
opts: Scouts dance fewer circuits each time they return, so only homes that keep winning new scouts stay alive
The queen stops her
The poor hollow shrinks
Other scouts cannot see her
items.why: A scout's dancing fades with each trip. A good hollow keeps bringing in new scouts, who dance for it as well. A poor hollow does not, so its dances fade away.

items.p: Scientists have shown that resting ants are useless, so colonies would do better with fewer of them.
items.why: False. Scientists have not shown this. The resting ants may be a reserve, they may be taking turns to rest, or they may be doing something we cannot see.

items.p: Scientists argue about why the resting ants in a colony are resting.

views.says: They are ready. If a lot of work arrives, they can join in at once.
Workers get tired, so a colony does better if different ants rest at different times.
They are doing something we cannot see, such as checking the nest or sharing smell.

items.ask: Which idea do you find most believable? What would you watch for in a nest to test it?
items.a: Any view with a test, such as watching whether the same ants always rest, or whether still ants join in when there is a lot of food.
items.why: Nobody has settled this, so there is no single right answer. A good answer picks one idea and suggests a way to test it, such as marking ants and following them.

items.p: Draw a termite mound cut in half. Show the queen's chamber, a fungus garden, and a tunnel with a soldier in it.
items.a: A mound shape with tunnels. In the middle, a chamber with a large queen. Beside it, a garden of small round balls with a fungus on them. In one tunnel, a soldier with a large head.
items.why: A strong drawing shows each chamber as part of one nest, with the soldier at the tunnel, the fungus where the workers farm, and the queen in the middle.
items.art: A blank mound-shaped outline on a page.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a termite mound. Label the three parts: the fungus garden, the queen's chamber, and the soldier in a tunnel.
a: Fungus garden: where workers grow the food for the colony
Queen's chamber: where the queen lays eggs
Soldier in a tunnel: where a soldier blocks a tunnel with her head
items.why: Each part of the mound has a job. The garden feeds the colony, the chamber holds the queen, and the soldier guards the tunnel.
items.art: A cut-away drawing of a termite mound with three marked places: a garden of round balls, a large chamber with a big termite, and a tunnel with a termite with a dark head.

items.p: A scientist wants to test whether bees follow a dancer's message, or only the flower smell on her body. Which test would give the clearest answer?
opts: Make the dancer point the wrong way and see where the new bees go
Count the dancer's waggles
Ask the beekeeper which flowers are in bloom
Feed all the bees the same sugar
items.why: If the new bees fly to the place the dance describes, and not to the place with the flower smell, the dance carries the message. This is what James Gould's trick showed in 1975.

items.p: A friend says, 'A bee's whole life is decided on the day she hatches.' Use one fact from this unit to disagree. Then say one thing we still do not know.
items.a: A honeybee worker does many jobs as she ages, and she can start foraging early if the hive lost its foragers. So her life is not set on the day she hatches. We still do not know why workers help raise their mother's young instead of having their own.
items.why: A strong answer gives one fact that fits, such as age-based jobs or early foraging, and one honest open question, such as why workers help or why resting ants rest.

items.p: Match each question to what we know about it.
pairs: The waggle dance tells direction and distance
Why workers help raise their mother's young
Naked mole-rats live with a queen
items.why: Some ideas have been tested again and again, and are settled. Others still have scientists on different sides, so they are debated.

quiz.p: Which of these is a eusocial society?
opts: A hive with one queen and thousands of workers who almost never lay eggs
A herd of cattle in a field
A flock of crows at a rubbish heap
A school of fish in a river
quiz.why: In a eusocial society only a few animals lay eggs, and many others look after the young and do the work. Cattle, crows and fish live in groups, but most adults can breed.

quiz.p: A team splits a three-step job so that each person does one step again and again. What is the main thing they gain?
opts: Less time lost swapping tools and more practice at each step
Each step becomes easier for the whole world
Nobody ever needs to learn another step
The team makes the job longer
quiz.why: Doing one step over and over saves the time of changing from one step to another and gives practice. The cost is that if the one person who knows a step is missing, that step stops.

quiz.p: If every member of a team can only do one job, the whole team can stop working when one member is missing.
quiz.why: True. When each job belongs to only one member, nobody else can do it. Hives avoid this risk because bees can change jobs when the hive needs it.

quiz.p: Which list shows the usual order of jobs for a worker honeybee as she grows older?
opts: Cleaning cells, feeding grubs, building and storing, guarding, foraging
Foraging, guarding, building, feeding grubs, cleaning cells
Guarding, cleaning cells, foraging, feeding grubs, building
Building, foraging, cleaning cells, guarding, feeding grubs
quiz.why: A worker starts in the middle of the hive with the safest jobs and ends outside with the most dangerous. The ages are only a guide.

quiz.p: A scientist takes all the foragers from a hive, and soon sees bees only a week old flying out for nectar. What does this show?
opts: A bee's job is not fixed to her age, and the hive's needs can change it
Bees can fly only when they are a week old
Young bees prefer to forage
The hive had too many nurses
quiz.why: Young bees began foraging early because the hive needed it. So age gives the usual order of jobs, but needs can change the order.

quiz.p: On the comb, a honeybee runs a waggle run that leans 30 degrees to the left of straight up. What does this tell the other bees?
opts: The food is 30 degrees to the left of the Sun's direction
The food is 30 metres away
The food is straight up in the air
The food is behind the hive
quiz.why: Straight up on the comb stands for the Sun's direction, so the angle of the run from straight up is the angle of the food from the Sun. The length of the waggle tells the distance.

quiz.p: One dancer waggles for half a second, and another waggles for three seconds. What does this show?
opts: The second bee found a place much farther away
The first bee found a place farther away
Both found places the same distance away
The second bee is older
quiz.why: A longer waggle run means a longer distance. In some honeybees, about one second has meant roughly a kilometre, though it differs between kinds.

quiz.p: What must happen before a honeybee swarm leaves its resting place and flies to a new home?
opts: About fifteen scouts gather at the same new home
The queen points to a home
The oldest bee leads the way
All the scouts agree at once
quiz.why: This number is the quorum. When about fifteen scouts are at one place, they signal back, and the swarm flies. The scouts do not all have to agree at the start, and the queen takes no part in choosing.

quiz.p: Why does it matter that each scout flies to a site herself before she dances for it?
opts: Each dance then comes from a real check, and not just a copy of another bee
It makes her dance for longer
It keeps her from getting lost
It makes the queen happy
quiz.why: If scouts only copied each other, one mistake could spread to the whole swarm. Independent checks make the swarm's choice more likely to be good.

quiz.p: Why does a group's middle guess often beat most single guesses of a number?
opts: Guesses that are too high and guesses that are too low tend to cancel each other
The middle guess is always the true number
The biggest guess is always right
Groups know more facts than single people
quiz.why: Mistakes that point in different directions cancel when you take the middle. The middle guess is not always right, but it is often better than most single guesses.

quiz.p: Everyone in a crowd looks at a jar that is lit in a way that makes it look smaller than it is, so everyone guesses too low. What will the middle guess probably be?
opts: Too low as well
Exactly right
Too high
Impossible to work out
quiz.why: A crowd can cancel mistakes that go in different directions, but not a mistake that everyone shares. When all guesses are too low, the middle guess is too low too.

quiz.p: How does a guard honeybee at the hive door tell a hive-mate from a stranger?
opts: By the smell of the colony on her body
By her colour
By a password dance
By her size
quiz.why: Every colony has its own smell, from the oily coat on the bodies of its members. A guard sniffs each arriving bee and lets in only those with the colony's smell.

open_questions.q: Why do the workers in some societies give up having their own young?

open_questions.q: Why are so many ants in a nest standing still?

maths.problem: A girl in Class 4 did the job of 12 paper squares one at a time in 144 seconds. She did the same job one step at a time in 120 seconds. How much time per square did the second way save? How much would it save over 300 squares?
maths.answer: 2 seconds per square, and 600 seconds over 300 squares. That is 10 minutes.
maths.explain: 144 minus 120 is 24 seconds saved over 12 squares. 24 divided by 12 is 2 seconds each. For 300 squares, 300 times 2 is 600 seconds, and 600 divided by 60 is 10 minutes.
maths.context: In the Switch or Stay test you time two ways of doing a three-step job and compare the totals.
maths.why_maths: A small saving on each item adds up to a large saving over many items, which is why splitting jobs pays off when there are many items to make.

maths.problem: A honeybee dancer waggles for 3 seconds. Take one second of waggle to mean about 1 kilometre. A bee flies about 6 metres in one second. About how long will the flight to the flowers take?
maths.answer: About 500 seconds, which is 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
maths.explain: 3 seconds of waggle means about 3 kilometres, which is 3,000 metres. 3,000 divided by 6 is 500 seconds. 500 seconds is 8 minutes and 20 seconds, because 8 times 60 is 480.
maths.context: A honeybee's waggle dance tells other bees how far away a place is by how long she waggles.
maths.why_maths: Turning kilometres into metres and metres into seconds shows how long a bee spends on a trip, and why a hive cares about which flowers are close.

maths.problem: On the comb, a dancer's waggle run leans 90 degrees to the right of straight up. Straight up stands for the Sun's direction. In the morning the Sun is in the east. If you face the Sun, in which direction is the food?
maths.explain: Facing east, your right hand points south. A turn of 90 degrees to the right from east is south. If the run leaned 90 degrees to the left, the food would be north.
maths.context: In the Dance the Map activity you use an angle on a paper comb to point the way to a hidden sweet.
maths.why_maths: An angle is a way to describe a direction without pointing. A bee uses an angle to send a direction to other bees in the dark.

maths.problem: In The Swarm Chooses game, the cup holds 3 moong dal, 5 chana and 12 rajma beans. A scout draws one pulse without looking. What fraction of the pulses in the cup are rajma, in simplest form? Which site is most likely to be visited next?
maths.answer: 3 out of 5, written 3/5. Site C, the rajma site, is the most likely.
maths.explain: The cup holds 3 plus 5 plus 12, which is 20 pulses. Rajma is 12 of them. 12 over 20 simplifies to 3 over 5, by dividing both numbers by 4. Rajma has the biggest share, so it is the most likely draw.
maths.context: In The Swarm Chooses game, pulses in a cup stand for scouts, and the more of one kind there are, the more likely the next scout is to visit that site.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how likely each draw is. It also shows why a site that gets an early lead tends to grow: the more of its pulses there are, the more often it is drawn.

maths.problem: Seven people guessed the number of chana in a glass: 150, 180, 200, 210, 240, 260 and 330. The true number was 220. What was the middle guess, and how far was it from the true number? Which two guesses were furthest from the true number?
maths.answer: The middle guess was 210, which is 10 away from 220. The furthest were 330, which is 110 away, and 150, which is 70 away.
maths.explain: The guesses are already in order, and the fourth one is the middle: 210. 220 minus 210 is 10. For 330, 330 minus 220 is 110. For 150, 220 minus 150 is 70.
maths.context: In the Jar of Dal test, a group guesses a number and you compare the middle guess with the true number.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order and finding the middle one is a quick way to summarise a group of guesses and to see which are far off.

maths.problem: A made-up worker honeybee lives 40 days. She is a cleaner for days 1 to 3, a nurse for days 4 to 10, a builder and storer for days 11 to 18, a guard for days 19 to 21 and a forager from day 22 to day 40. What fraction of her life is spent building and storing, in simplest form? What fraction is spent foraging?
maths.answer: Building and storing is 1/5 of her life. Foraging is 19/40.
maths.explain: Days 11 to 18 are 8 days. 8 out of 40 simplifies to 1 out of 5, by dividing both by 8. Foraging is days 22 to 40, which is 19 days. 19 out of 40 cannot be made simpler.
maths.context: In the activity A Bee's Forty Days you draw a worker honeybee's jobs along a timeline of 40 days.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of a life each job takes, so you can compare jobs of different lengths.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people watched bees return to the hive and saw only a busy crowd. In the 1940s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch painted dots on bees and watched them through glass in a hive. He saw that a bee who had found food ran in a straight line while shaking her body, then circled back and ran again. By measuring her runs, he worked out that the angle shows the direction of the food, and the length of the run shows how far. Not everyone believed him. In the 1960s some scientists said the other bees were only following the flower smell on the dancer's body, and that the dance meant nothing. In 1975 James Gould tricked dancers into pointing the wrong way, and the new bees flew to the place the dance described, not to the food. In 2005 scientists tracked recruits with tiny radar tags and saw them fly to the place the dancer described.
how_we_found_out.who: Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist (1886 to 1982)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought the dance meant nothing and that bees find food by smell alone. When dancers were made to point the wrong way, the new bees followed the dance, which showed that the dance carries the message.

roots.context: We have seen a hive share its jobs, a dance carry a map and a swarm choose a home. Now we ask what a hive shows about being one thing and being many.

deep_truth.truth: In a hive, one bee does many jobs in turn, from cleaning to finding food. When a hive loses many foragers, young bees start foraging early. So a job is not what a bee is. It is what the hive needs from her today.
deep_truth.habit: We say worker, nurse, guard and soldier as if each were a kind of animal, the way we say 'teacher' as if that word were a person's whole self. In honeybees the word names a stage, not a kind. In some termites and ants, soldiers do have a different body and keep one job.
deep_truth.evidence: Marked bees were followed from the day they hatched, and each did one job after another as she aged. When older bees were taken away, some young bees started foraging days or weeks early. In Switch or Stay you also found that changing jobs costs time, which is one reason a hive keeps each job for days at a time.

three.who_am_i: Your body is a society of about 37 trillion cells, and each kind has a job. None of them could live alone for long, just like a worker bee.
three.what_is_life: Living is not one fixed job. A bee, a wasp or a cell changes what they do as the body or the colony needs.
three.what_is_this_world: Many things we call one thing, such as a hive, a forest or a body, are many beings who depend on each other. Where one ends and the next begins depends on where we draw the line.

roots.thread: No honeybee sees the whole hive. Each one knows only the cell in front of her, the smell at the door or the dance she is following. Yet the hive keeps its warmth, feeds its young and picks a home. The whole does things that none of its parts is doing. Some sages taught that the world is like this too, with many beings who each see a little, inside one whole that nobody stands outside of.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased, the last hymn of the Rig Veda says, come together, speak together, let your minds know alike. It is a hymn for people gathered to decide something together.

teachings.teaching: Parasparopagraho jivanam. Living beings help one another. The Jain tradition teaches that all life holds together because every being supports others.

science.text: Honeybees keep the middle of the nest at about 34 to 35 degrees Celsius. The whole colony does this together, and no single bee holds the temperature.
Many scientists think the first animal bodies began as colonies of single cells that stayed together and started to share jobs. Fossils cannot show it, so it remains an idea.

other_view.view: A hive is a lot of separate bees, each following her own rules. 'The hive decides' is only a short way to say what the bees do together. They say that a hive does not want anything, and only the bees do.
